title: [Webinar] Target Intelligence: An Ethical Hacker’s Perspective on Exposed Data and Social Engineering
summary: Join Optery’s Paul Mander and ethical hacker Manit Sahib to learn how attackers use exposed data for workforce reconnaissance and social engineering.
body_markdown:
## See what attackers can learn about your workforce before they ever make contact.


## Full Transcript


**Paul Mander (0:05):** All right, good morning, good afternoon, and good evening, depending on where you are. Thanks for joining us for today’s webinar. My name is Paul Mander, and I’m Chief Commercial Officer and GM of Optery for Business.


A few housekeeping items before we begin. We will be taking questions at the end of the webinar, so if you have questions, please ask them using the Q&A feature in Zoom. We’ll also be sending the recording of the webinar to all attendees afterward, in case you have to hop off early.


I’m really excited to have this webinar today. I’m sure many of you have attended webinars and had conversations about social engineering, and a lot of them focus on defense: what tactics and tools to deploy when an attacker makes contact with your infrastructure. For the next 40 or so minutes, we’re going to look at things much earlier in the life cycle. We’re going to look at what attackers are learning about enterprises, and the people who work at those enterprises, during the reconnaissance phase of an attack, and how that reconnaissance helps shape the attack itself.


There’s maybe no better person to discuss that with me today than Manit Sahib. The resume speaks for itself. Defending UK SWIFT payment systems is probably one of the most important cybersecurity jobs in the world. But Manit, I’ll turn it over to you so you can introduce yourself to our audience.


**Manit Sahib (1:32):** Yeah, thanks, Paul. Hi, everyone. I’m Manit Sahib. I’m an offensive security expert and the CEO of Cytadel. We help organizations test their defenses against AI-driven attacks, such as ransomware, and AI-enabled fraud, such as phishing and deepfakes. As you can see, I’m the former head of penetration testing and red teaming for the UK’s central bank, the Bank of England, and I’m certified by the National Cyber Security Centre here in the UK. If I’m not hacking, I’m in the gym. My current tagline is: I hack companies before criminals do, then I tell the board what would have happened.


**Paul Mander (2:10):** Please tell me you wear a T-shirt that says that while you’re at the gym.


**Manit Sahib (2:15):** \[laughs\] I should do. Hashtag.


## What attackers do during reconnaissance (2:20)


**Paul Mander (2:20):** All right, let’s jump into this. I don’t know if this is your experience, Manit, but it’s certainly been ours on the Optery side, and maybe in the industry in general: a lot of cybersecurity practitioners view reconnaissance as something that happens upstream. This isn’t the attack hitting me. It’s happening beforehand, and it’s a little bit separate. I would argue that the whole industry is better served by thinking of the attack as beginning during reconnaissance. Reconnaissance should be thought of as part of the attack itself, and I think organizations are going to be served better with their practitioners thinking that way.


But I really want to hear from you, Manit. Before an attacker begins a social engineering attack and makes contact with anyone, what are they doing during the reconnaissance phase?


**Manit Sahib (3:16):** Great question, Paul. Let’s set the scene a little and explain why reconnaissance is so important. Recon allows you to map the surface area of your target. By understanding the attack surface, you can plan the best attack vector to achieve the objective. From an attacker’s perspective, the objective is commonly to steal money, encrypt data, or exfiltrate data. For us ethical hackers, the good guys, the objective is to be in a position to steal money or access data, but go no further. But the reconnaissance is the same for both the good guys and the bad guys. Fundamentally, recon allows us to map the target and craft a suitable attack vector to achieve the objective. If you fail to do reconnaissance properly, everything downstream is impacted. As a simple example, if we target the wrong user or the wrong IP, we could be attacking the wrong company, and we don’t want to be doing that.


Coming back to your question: as an attacker, what do I want to learn about the target? We commonly target organizations. From an organization and technical stack perspective, we want to know what defenses are in place: what kind of security products they have, the number of devices, and the number of users. You also commonly see third-party dependencies. If there’s a weakness in a third party, we go toward that rather than attacking the target directly.


Then we move on to the human element, which is why we’re all here. If I’m targeting someone, I want to know which department they’re in, which time zone, and which permissions they might have on the network. Because we use humans for social engineering, we have to go deeper on the reconnaissance. One thing for us as attackers is knowing who we want to target. The next thing is that we need to craft a pretext to convince the target to engage. For those who don’t know, a pretext is a believable story that I provide to an individual to gain their trust.


When we do reconnaissance to craft pretexts, I want to know everything about the person. I want to know where they live, what their interests are, what they’re posting on social media, whether they like cats or dogs, whether they go to conferences. The more information I have, the better the story, the more likely I am to gain their trust, and the more likely I am to compromise them.


**Paul Mander (5:50):** Got it. So is it something like, if the company’s Instagram account posted a picture of the holiday party, an attacker says, “Oh, that could be my hook for my phishing email.” Is that an example?


**Manit Sahib (5:57):** Yes. Thinking off the cuff here, I could pretend to be the photography company they hired for the event and say, “Hey, guys, here are the new pictures. Why don’t you download them?” Then I’ll put a link in there. I’ve already gained their trust, because they’re looking at something they’re already subconsciously aware of. And it’s practically guaranteed someone is going to click, thinking, “Oh, did I do something silly at the party?”


**Paul Mander (6:28):** Yeah. That was probably one of the most memorable phishing trainings I had in a past life. It was literally right after a holiday party, someone pretending to be the head of HR with a fake Google Drive link. But it’s certainly a very viable path for a threat actor.


So they do this reconnaissance. You find out when the holiday party is, you do the technical infrastructure assessment like you said, but then there’s really the people element. I need to know who to contact. We touched on knowing about the company, but there are a lot of places threat actors can go. We mentioned social media. There are data broker sites, there’s breach data, and maybe company websites. If we look at this menu of data sources, what does each of them contribute? And from your experience, are there ones threat actors find more helpful for their purposes than others?


**Manit Sahib (7:23):** Social media is a gold mine, whether it’s pictures or badges. I’ve seen people post pictures on Instagram with their badges showing, and I’m like, “Let me zoom in on that.” I’ll take it to my ID printer, go to their site, and say, “Oh, my ID doesn’t work.” And the number of times security says, “Okay, just go in,” or “We’ll print you a new pass.” So social media is what I normally use.


LinkedIn is where I start. It gives me the name, location, and maybe education of the target. You could even go wider and say, for this organization I’m targeting, I want to know all the employees who work in treasury, for example. It will give me a list of, let’s say, 20 people. Then I will go and take that list over to data brokers, because data brokers enrich that data. It will give me things like the home address of people, phone numbers, even email addresses. I’ve found that in some cases, data brokers even give me other social media accounts. Maybe they’ve linked the person’s Instagram, which doesn’t have that public attribution on the general internet, but the data brokers have it. Because I have this information, it helps me create the pretext, the believable story I’m going to use to attack people.


In addition, what I find on data brokers allows me to find the target’s associations. What you’ll commonly find with an executive in a high-level position at an enterprise company is that they have a relatively small footprint. So I’ll put them into a data broker and find their associations: family, relatives, children, all the people connected to them. It’s practically guaranteed one of them has a big social media presence. I will then target that individual, build trust with them, and then indirectly target my actual target.


## Breach data and infostealer credentials (9:27)


**Paul Mander (9:27):** Gotcha. What I found interesting in everything you said, and we did a study about this earlier this year, is breach data. You didn’t mention anything about breach data, and I’m curious where you feel it fits in. In our study, breach data wasn’t that high on the list either. But many people think of it as the first thing: “Oh, my data is on the dark web,” or something like that. You didn’t mention it in the planning path you just described.


**Manit Sahib (9:53):** It’s a good observation. There’s breach data, and then there’s credential stealer data, which we can talk about because it’s on your list there. The reason I don’t typically use breach data is because it’s old. Once I’ve found email addresses from the data brokers, or linked from LinkedIn, I’ll put them into breach sources to find out what their password was. Because this data is old, that password is not going to be in use, so it’s not going to be valid for a credential reuse attack or anything like that.


What I will use it for, down the line, is as a pretext: “Hey, I’m from security. I’ve seen this password come up. Can you confirm you’ve changed it? Click this link to confirm it’s been changed.” Once they click it, boom, you’re in. So I’m using breach data as a pretext rather than as a source to gain more information.


**Paul Mander (10:56):** That makes sense. I guess there’s a TTL for the usefulness of the breach data. A new breach is perhaps more useful for threat actors, versus your contact information and relationship information, which is static. That doesn’t change. So you go to a data broker, and if they collected it years ago, it’s still going to be useful for someone.


**Manit Sahib (11:19):** Yeah. And then you’ve got credential stealer information, which has really valuable information. If a device has been compromised by well-known stealers, like RedLine Stealer, and there’s a whole number of them, threat actors will publish the stealer online; it will infect loads of machines, and it will extract all the credentials you’ve got stored, for example, in Google. When Google says “Save the password,” do not save the password in Google. Use a password manager. The stealer is able to extract those credentials, and then they get published. From that data, you’ll see logins for different websites, maybe portals for organizations. So credential stealer information is quite important as well.


## Channels: personal devices, LinkedIn and multi-channel attacks (12:11)


**Paul Mander (12:11):** Gotcha. So they’re obtaining the information as you described. The threat actor is looking to attack an organization, and the goal is to get money, as you were saying, because companies have money. But what threat actors are obtaining is people’s personal phone numbers and personal emails. That’s what they’re getting from data brokers and using to reach employees, maybe outside the corporate environment. That’s just one example, and attacking the corporate environment- the corporate email, the corporate phones, and so forth- is certainly part of it as well. With all these different channels threat actors can use, have you found that they use them in different ways, or that there’s a set of priorities where they’ll pick one channel over another first?


**Manit Sahib (13:07):** I love this as an attack vector. In the industry, we call it phishing via services, and it’s “via services” because these services are outside organizational control. We don’t have defenses on LinkedIn or Instagram that monitor what attachments you get. As an attacker, I commonly use… \[laughs\] I’m informing the bad guys there. I commonly use LinkedIn because I know, as an employee, it’s acceptable to go on LinkedIn at work. So I will send attachments through LinkedIn, because it’s not scanned through your email gateway or your web gateway. It’s a common channel we’re seeing. I’ve been involved in incident response for people targeted on WhatsApp and LinkedIn, even LinkedIn DMs. You see lateral movement from personal social media accounts that then compromises the environment. It’s a common channel, and we’re seeing it more and more: attackers using personal emails and personal devices, whether it’s WhatsApp, text messages, or even phone calls on personal devices, to get that lateral movement into the corporation.


**Paul Mander (14:29):** Yeah, and that LinkedIn example is quite the visibility gap. As you said, all the infrastructure you’ve got doesn’t really help with that. How should organizations think about it? Is forbidding BYOD the goal, and the corporate laptop just locks down LinkedIn, anything like that? What are your thoughts?


**Manit Sahib (14:44):** The problem is that even on a corporate laptop, you’re still going to allow LinkedIn, because HR might use it for recruitment, or marketing might use it. It is a challenge, because we do need these platforms, but there’s no security product for LinkedIn. There isn’t much you can do. It would be to reduce the footprint: reduce the social media footprint of executives or VIPs, which we can touch on a little more. But you’re limited in what you can do.


**Paul Mander (15:25):** I’m probably putting you on the spot a little here, but you mentioned LinkedIn, and sales and marketing folks use LinkedIn quite a bit. One approach is to set up a multi-channel campaign: email a prospect, send them a text message, and so on. Have you seen threat actors use this sort of multi-channel approach, where it’s an SMS plus a LinkedIn request or an email?


**Manit Sahib (15:52):** You’re giving away all the techniques. \[laughs\] Since we’re sharing golden nuggets: what I would commonly do is set up a thread. I’ll have two or three different people, all fake, having their own conversation. Then they’ll bring the target into the thread with an urgent request. Now you’re putting the target under pressure, and there’s a whole thread waiting for them, so they want to respond straight away. You’re bringing in urgency, and you’re bringing other people into the mix.


**Paul Mander (16:24):** And are the people in that thread impersonations? Like, “Let me pull in the CFO,” and then the CEO and CTO are in there talking about something? Is that the sort of example you mean?


**Manit Sahib (16:36):** Yes, exactly. They’re all in there, but they’re all made up. They look legitimate because you’ve cloned the profiles. It’s all a pretext we’ve already defined before we contact the target.


**Paul Mander (16:48):** Wow. Multi-channel marketing, for both the good guys and the bad guys, it seems.


**Manit Sahib (16:54):** If I were thinking about another startup idea, it would be looking at phishing via services, and specifically LinkedIn, because a lot of enterprises are seeing it as an entry point, especially in the incident response exercises I’m involved in. You see it whether it’s Instagram or LinkedIn.


**Paul Mander (17:13):** Yeah. We are social creatures by nature. Arguments aside, that’s why social media took off. LinkedIn is interesting because folks like you and me who do these sorts of webinars have a presence there. It’s part of what we need to do. But it’s definitely a gold mine for threat actors in terms of reconnaissance. It’s also a channel people pay attention to, because my next job offer might be on LinkedIn, or someone I follow in the industry is always sharing interesting things, so I’m checking LinkedIn.


**Manit Sahib (17:58):** I’m going to get a load of PDFs sent to me on LinkedIn after this. \[laughs\] If you’re sending me an attachment, I’m not going to open it. Put it in text.


**Paul Mander (18:06):** Yeah, exactly. It’s the same thing: don’t open an attachment from someone you don’t know in your email. Of course, we’ve got tooling to help with that. The same thing applies on LinkedIn, but just being in that channel, I think the human tendency is that whatever training and knowledge you might have is lessened because you’re in that specific channel.


**Manit Sahib (18:31):** Yeah, and I think you touch on a good point there about training, because more and more organizations are doing advanced cyber awareness training that looks at things like social media and campaigns like the multi-person thread I talked about. So when an individual is contacted, they’re already aware that it could be malicious.


**Paul Mander (19:01):** Yeah. Training is not foolproof, but it’s very, very important. It’s maybe the last line of defense, if you will.


## Which roles get targeted (19:10)


**Paul Mander (19:10):** So we’re on LinkedIn, we’ve used data brokers to find out how to contact people, and we’ve got these multi-channel campaigns going with LinkedIn and SMS. I think we’ve really set up the attack flow. When threat actors do that reconnaissance, they have a ton of data at their fingertips, and one of the data sources is org charts. Multiple security researchers are citing places like ZoomInfo, and data on ZoomInfo is a very big threat because you essentially have the whole organization chart there.


Going back to the survey I mentioned: we surveyed a bunch of enterprise CISOs earlier this year, and they told us their IT team was the most targeted group within the company, followed by HR. So with all the data available to them, threat actors are choosing the IT and HR functions to target. From your experience, Manit, do you see the same, or have you found that other roles might be more valuable, and potentially why?


**Manit Sahib (20:18):** Firstly, I love the breakdown you’ve done. I think everybody should be looking at their organization by department and thinking about the attack surface this way. It’s not just generic attacks on humans. You have to break it down like you have, because for each of these departments, as an attacker, I craft the attack differently. For finance or treasury, I’m going for the money movements, whereas with IT I’m looking at disrupting their backups or holding their data for ransom. So my campaign would be very different. I think the breakdown you’ve done here is really good.


From what I’m seeing in hands-on experience, I would put help desk as number one. The reason I say this is because if you look at the attacks on retail in the UK- Harrods, Co-op, and M&S- they were all phishing attacks: voice phishing- phoning someone up, all on the help desk, to reset passwords. If you look at MGM, the casino hack, that was on the help desk as well. Same attack technique: on the phone to the help desk, “Can you reset my password?” One of the biggest attacks in history we’ve had, Jaguar Land Rover, was something like a 1.9 billion breach, and taxpayers had to pay it out as well. Same thing: an attack on the help desk via phishing. So I would put help desk as number one, and then I would probably put finance, which I class as treasury. So finance and treasury as number two.


**Paul Mander (22:00):** Yeah. The credit for this goes to the industry. We just consolidated the data. This is what CISOs said is happening within their organizations, and hopefully sharing it helps people become more educated about it.


Finance is an interesting one. There’s that well-known case of a person, I think in California, who essentially got millions of dollars from Google and Meta by targeting finance with fake invoices, which were being paid. The threat actor made off with a few million dollars before he finally got caught. So finance, well, they control the purse strings, so that one usually jumps out.


Executives are pretty low on the list. My theory is that, one, there’s a lot more protection around them, but two, executives are just so busy that they don’t respond as much to random things. But on your point about help desk: that’s low on the list, but you shared some really big examples, MGM being one of the biggest globally.


**Manit Sahib (23:04):** Yeah. And just on finance: you see more attacks using synthetic media, like voice cloning and deepfakes. There’s that CFO who got cloned on a Teams call, and the employee paid.


**Paul Mander (23:18):** Oh, the one in Hong Kong, right?


**Manit Sahib (23:21):** It’s funny, because there have been quite a few. I think two or three got compromised for the same amount, $25 million, with the same kind of technique. So in finance and treasury, you’re seeing synthetic media used with executives.


Number three: this isn’t what I’ve seen other attackers do, but what I would do, and again I’m sharing some golden nuggets here. I would not target an executive. I would target the executive’s assistant, because they have delegation permissions on the executive’s mailbox. They can act on behalf of the executive; they’ll have reduced security controls, or at least not as elevated as the executive’s, and they definitely won’t have data broker removal or OSINT removal done the way an executive would. So I think executive assistants are a good one as well.


**Paul Mander (24:16):** Yeah. One thing you mentioned earlier I want to go back to. You said that when you’re doing reconnaissance, you start on LinkedIn to find out where I work and my education. What specifically about a target’s education is important from a threat actor’s perspective?


**Manit Sahib (24:34):** It’s about aggregating the data. I want to enrich my data, and I want to make sure the person I’m going to target is the one I’m getting the data for. What I’ve found is that the education from LinkedIn helps validate the information from the data broker. I think that’s a really valid question, because education plays a big part when I search on data brokers.


**Paul Mander (25:02):** Oh, got it. So it’s less about, “Hey, I went to the University of Michigan,” and more that it helps you refine and improve your data quality as a threat actor.


**Manit Sahib (25:14):** Exactly.


**Paul Mander (25:16):** Yeah. I think that’s not discussed enough. Data brokers are a threat, but they also don’t always have the most accurate data, which in some ways serves the good guys well. If something’s incorrect on my data broker profile, I’m cool with that, because it misdirects threat actors. But they’re consolidating data because of that. I think threat actors know that, and the example you gave about education is very interesting: they’re using it to correct or enrich the data, if you will.


**Manit Sahib (25:47):** Yeah. That’s what I do, and I guarantee the other guys are doing it too. There was one thing I wanted to add on help desk, and this is for the audience to be aware of as well, because I’d put help desk at number one for two reasons. One, because they’re getting phone calls to reset passwords, and we’re seeing attackers change their techniques now. From what I’m aware of, in the organizations I work with, help desks have deployed policies that say, “You need to give me your line manager’s information before I can reset your password.” So we’re seeing staged attacks: first on HR, to find out the individual’s manager, then a second attack on the help desk saying, “Can you reset my password? This is my line manager’s name and number.”


Resetting passwords is one aspect. And again, I don’t want to give more information to the bad guys, but here’s what I have done. Help desk users in an Active Directory or enterprise environment are set up to manage and create accounts. That’s their sole purpose, whether it’s for executives or admins. If you look at how the permissions are set up in Active Directory, help desk users have delegation rights on all the users they create. So if I compromise one help desk user, I can now use my permissions to access any account.


**Paul Mander (27:34):** Wow.


**Manit Sahib (27:35):** So that’s why I would put help desk as number one. For me, I get the most value from it.


**Paul Mander (27:44):** Yeah. They have access to the most valuable keys. You mentioned we’re letting all the bad guys know, but I think we have more good guys on this call than bad guys.


**Manit Sahib (27:56):** I hope so.


**Paul Mander (27:57):** The more the good guys are aware of these things, the better. Help desk might be the sleeper there. CISOs are saying it’s less targeted, but that’s potentially changing, and some of the high-profile examples you shared show it being successfully targeted.


## AI and social engineering (28:18)


**Paul Mander (28:18):** All right. It’s October 2026, so we can’t have a webinar where we don’t discuss AI. For all the cybersecurity practitioners on this call, we’re in a particularly interesting news cycle about AI and cyber right now, and I thank everyone who might be taking a break from dealing with PHP **\[unclear\]** to discuss social engineering with Manit and me. But AI hype aside, Manit, have you actually seen an example of a threat actor using AI in social engineering to do something that would have been difficult, or maybe impossible, without AI?


**Manit Sahib (28:59):** Offensive AI is my forte. I could speak about this all day long. We are seeing evidence of autonomous AI attacks in the industry. Two years ago, I created my presentation and research on AI-driven ransomware: how it can compromise an environment within five and a half minutes, which is 550 times faster than ransomware gangs. Today I train different AI agents to do specific roles: recon, entry, exfiltration, encryption, the whole attack chain. I think the whole industry was maybe asleep at that point, or didn’t believe it was happening.


Then in November last year, we saw Anthropic release their report about a Chinese state actor compromising 17 organizations using this kind of autonomous AI attack. We’re seeing it even more commonly now. Even OpenAI has released some details about attacks they’re seeing that use ChatGPT. Recently, ransomware groups- I think it was Gentlemen or Inc ransomware- have used AI as part of their toolkit.


Importantly, AI has lowered the barrier to entry for criminals.


**Paul Mander (30:18):** Sure.


**Manit Sahib (30:20):** This means less sophisticated people can conduct these attacks at speed and scale. Right now, we know from the industry that attackers are ahead of defenses. When the Hugging Face hack happened **\[unclear\]** , even Hugging Face said, “We need more telemetry of attacks happening so we can improve our defenses.”


If you take all of this to the social engineering, reconnaissance, and AI side, here’s something interesting I’m sure everyone will enjoy. One of my first talks was on research into how we can use AI for reconnaissance, compromise an account, bypass MFA, and achieve complete account takeover of an individual. About 18 months ago, I created my own AI hacking agent for phishing. This was to strengthen defenses for the likes of M&S, Harrods, and JLR, all the organizations that got hit. I thought, “This is happening. What if we could create a tool that simulates these attacks, is AI-driven, and doesn’t need me to be part of it?”


To explain a little about what happens: it does recon, so it finds a list of targets on LinkedIn. It then finds their phone numbers. I’ve trained an AI agent, so it’s an agent actually calling you, and it calls these targets simultaneously. It pretends to be from IT support or Microsoft support, depending on which campaign you get, and asks them to verify their account due to suspicious activity. I’ve made sure I’ve trained these agents to handle objections like a salesperson. If the victim says, “Oh, no, I’m not…,” the agent will say, “Oh, but did you travel somewhere?” It will look at their LinkedIn and see if they traveled somewhere. “Did you connect to some Wi-Fi? That could be your suspicious activity. We just need you to secure the account. Click the link.”


As soon as the user goes to the link and clicks it, they’re prompted to log in. I’ve combined this with Evilginx, which is a man-in-the-middle attack framework that not only compromises the password but also compromises your MFA token and steals your session token. All of this is done autonomously, without me being there. The goal was: hit the button, go to the gym. I can press the button, give it a list of targets, and it will call all these people and come back and show me how many accounts it compromised.


I presented this at SANS HackFest **\[unclear\]** , one of the hacking conferences. It got so much interest that I actually pulled my research down, because I’m not trying to help the bad guys. But I wanted to share one example of what is possible with AI and reconnaissance, and how we’re going to see more attacks on the human element. There’s a quote everyone uses at the moment: attackers don’t break in; they log in. And now, with agentic solutions, they’re looking at non-human identities. Identity is the attack surface. If I’m an attacker coming in, I don’t want to do recon, set up a command-and-control framework, deploy malware to a workstation, and move in stealth when I can just hit a button, compromise an identity, and have all the permissions of that user.


**Paul Mander (34:08):** Yeah. Pivoting a little toward solutions, which we’ll get to on the next slide: going back to your comment about Hugging Face, the response from Hugging Face was, “We need more telemetry data.” I found that response interesting, because it wasn’t “The solution is AI.” The solution is more telemetry. That’s cybersecurity 101: you always want more data, because with more telemetry data you have a better understanding of what’s going on within your infrastructure. It always starts with the data, and then maybe on top of that, AI can help you. But it was down to telemetry data, and having the right visibility could potentially have helped them, if not stop the attack, then maybe catch it sooner than they did.


## What security teams should focus on (35:03)


**Paul Mander (35:03):** So, solutions. We’ve spent the last half hour sharing the nuggets, like you’re saying, and hopefully there’s no threat actor watching this and formulating attacks as we speak. If someone on this webinar has heard everything we’ve been talking about and wants to do something about it, to make their employees or organization harder to target, what should they focus on?


**Manit Sahib (35:36):** How much money do they have? Buy all the tools. \[laughs\] No, do not do that. Do not buy overlapping tools.


Number one, I would say you need to understand your attack surface. This sounds so simple, but I can tell you the number of organizations I go into where I ask, “What are your external devices, your external assets?” and they say, “We’re not sure. We’re not sure who’s externally facing.” Examples of that are the Colonial Pipeline attack and also Microsoft, because both attacks were the same. With Colonial Pipeline, they had a user account that should have been deactivated, and a legacy VPN portal with no MFA challenge. As soon as a threat actor found the credential on a breach site, they used it. It should have been changed, but it was a user who should have been deactivated and offboarded. There was no MFA challenge, and they logged in. That’s how Colonial Pipeline got hacked. In January, I think January this year, Microsoft got hacked the same way. It was a test tenant that was exposed, with a user who should have been offboarded.


So these major organizations still have gaps. I get it. It’s so big. You’re trying to keep your CMDB, your asset register, up to date. So number one is know your external attack surface, technology definitely. Recently we saw the PHP **\[unclear\]** attack hit every organization. How many people scrambled and said, “Do we have PHP? Where is it? Does it impact a crown jewel?”


The second one is to map your crown jewels to these assets: your business-critical services. You need to be able to look upstream and downstream and say, “If this user is compromised, could they impact that crown jewel? Then you can get into the VIPs, which we spoke about before. VIPs could be people who have access to these crown jewels, whether it’s finance, backups, or developers, or if you’re building your own internal AI models, the people training the underlying data model. They are VIPs, because if someone compromised them, they could poison all the data in your AI models. Mapping that allows you to understand the business impact and the business risk.


We talked about more cyber awareness training, but one of the things I think is key is to test your defenses. Be proactive about security. Whether it’s a red team or a pen test, let a good guy attack you the way the bad guys would, because they’ll see things you make assumptions about. Once you have the results, you can act on them. One of the key things out of that might be, “I found this executive’s digital footprint,” and then you use data broker removal and OSINT removal to remove that data from the internet. But you need to understand where the gaps are before you can start remediating.
